input.question: Why are the engines on small airplanes (e.g. Cessnas) make such a different sound than engines in cars that have a similar horsepower rating?
input.ground_truth: Some of the sound difference certainly comes from the difference in design and some of it is the lower rpm but most of the sound you hear from a small airplane isn't the engine, it's the propeller. To get an idea what I'm talking about listen to the sound of a turboprop like a Cessna Caravan, the engine in that plane is a turbine (basically a jet engine) so the engine by itself makes a high pitched whine, but the prop is so noisy that it drowns out most of the engine noise.

Question: Why are the engines on small airplanes (e.g. Cessnas) make such a different sound than engines in cars that have a similar horsepower rating?

Okay, let’s imagine you have a toy car and a toy airplane. Both toys can go fast, but they sound really different, right?

The reason is because the way they make their engines work is different! 

A car’s engine is like a little spinning bike that goes round and round very, very fast. It makes a rumbling sound that you can feel in your chest.

An airplane’s engine, even if it’s not super big, is designed to push a lot of air really fast to help the airplane fly. It works a little bit like a fan that blows air very strongly. That’s why it makes a different, louder, sometimes “put-put-put” sound, not like the car.

So even if both have the same “strength” (horsepower), they are built for different jobs, and that’s why they sound different!
